rationale: The book's core—that works are simply deeds (not a synonym for obedience), becoming obedience only when they execute God's command (or disobedience under another lawgiver)—best unifies the printed texts without forcing them into a single soteriological slot. Exodus 18:20 defines 'the work that they must do' as the concrete deed taught alongside ordinances and the way to walk; Micah 6:16 treats the 'works of the house of Ahab' as deeds done under alien statutes; Psalm 111:7 pairs 'the works of his hands' with 'all his commandments'; Romans 4:4–5 uses the laborer's work as the wage-claiming act that creates debt rather than grace; James 2:21–22 uses Abraham's work as the deed that makes faith visible and perfect; Luke 17:7–10 shows that even the servant who has 'done all those things which are commanded' remains an unprofitable servant who has merely performed duty. These texts are explained more tightly by the book's distinction than by the common reading that immediately folds every occurrence into 'fruit/evidence of the heart' or 'basis of final judgment.' The common view correctly notes the evidential function in many passages but does not account for the wage-versus-duty contrast or the neutral status of the deed prior to the governing lawgiver; the book's core does so with fewer unsupported steps. Secondary claims (e.g., that works are always 'commandment-shaped') are elaborations that may be disputed without overturning the core referent.
book_core_identification: Works are deeds, not a synonym for obedience; a work becomes obedience when it executes God's command or disobedience when another lawgiver governs it.
book_secondary_elaborations: Romans 4 uses the laborer's work as the act offered for wages and debt
James 2 uses Abraham's work as faith made visible and perfected
Complete obedience still earns no wage; the servant has only done his duty (Luke 17:7–10)
Works are the commandment-shaped enactment of trust that living faith produces
strongest_counter_interpretation: Works are the outward deeds or actions that express and evidence the inner spiritual condition—good works the visible fruit of genuine faith/grace/regeneration, evil works the fruit of unbelief/flesh/darkness—functioning as the basis of divine assessment at judgment because they manifest the heart (with the Protestant caveat that they are not the meritorious cause of justification).
counter_core_identification: Outward deeds/actions that express and evidence the inner spiritual condition (good as fruit of faith, evil as fruit of unbelief).
material_core_denial: Does not deny that works are deeds, but blurs or omits the book's precise claim that 'works' is not a synonym for obedience and becomes obedience or disobedience only relative to the governing lawgiver; it also under-emphasizes the pure-duty (no-wage) status of even complete command-keeping.
counter_case: Matthew 7:16–20 and John 3:19–21 treat deeds as the fruit by which the tree/heart is known
Ephesians 2:8–10 and Titus 2:14; 3:8 place good works as the purpose and fruit of grace-created believers
James 2:14–26 and Revelation 20:12–13 use works as the visible demonstration and judgment criterion of living faith
Galatians 5:19–23 and Ephesians 5:11 contrast works of the flesh/darkness with the fruit of the Spirit
The Protestant framing (Romans 3:28; Galatians 2:16; Titus 3:5) keeps works as evidence rather than meritorious cause
book_explanatory_advantages: Directly accounts for Exodus 18:20's definition of 'the work that they must do' as the taught deed, not already labeled 'obedience'
Explains Micah 6:16's 'works of the house of Ahab' as deeds performed under alien statutes without importing an inner-condition gloss
Unifies Romans 4:4–5 (wage-debt work) and James 2:21–22 (faith-made-visible work) under one neutral referent 'deed' whose master and claim determine its status
Makes Luke 17:7–10's 'unprofitable servants' who have done all commanded a natural consequence rather than an awkward exception to a fruit-of-faith reading
Fits Psalm 111:7's parallel of God's works and His sure commandments without reducing works to a mere synonym of obedience
counter_explanatory_advantages: Covers the large body of 'tree known by fruit' and judgment-according-to-works texts more immediately
Aligns with the dominant Protestant and Catholic framing of good works as necessary fruit or cooperative grace without requiring the extra 'becomes obedience' step
Handles Johannine and apocalyptic 'I know your works' passages as spiritual-state diagnostics
unresolved_objections: The book does not fully engage the New-Perspective reading of 'works of the law' as covenant boundary markers
Secondary elaboration that works are always 'commandment-shaped' (via Rev 2:26) rests on additional symbolic moves not required by the core
Some judgment-by-works texts (e.g., Matt 25:31–46) remain more naturally read under the broader evidential counter
